1:
Barnes opens by naming the quarrel that runs through the chapter: few have been the subject of more decidedly different interpretations, and it is still discussed whether the apostle refers to his own experience before conversion or to the conflicts of a mind already renewed. The main design is not in doubt — to show the insufficiency of the law to produce peace of mind in a troubled sinner. Calvin explains why the argument had to be resumed: the question of the law's abrogation had been settled briefly, but it was difficult and bred further questions, so the apostle now shows at length how the law is abrogated with regard to us, since while it holds us bound to itself it can do nothing but condemn us.

The address is explained four ways. Gill takes it for the Jewish converts at Rome, and thinks brethren was chosen to soften their resentment, since they were zealous of the law. Wesley agrees the appeal is chiefly to Jews and adds the motive, that the apostle is weaning them from their fondness for the Mosaic law. Clarke gives the anxiety behind that fondness: they rested in the law as sufficient for justification, and to renounce it might appear a renunciation of their allegiance to God. Ellicott, reckoning the Roman church about equally Jewish and Gentile, explains how the Gentile half would know the law well enough for the argument to bite — from intercourse with the Jewish members and from hearing the Old Testament read in the synagogues. Robertson keeps it wider: Romans, whether Jews or Gentiles, knew the principle of law.

The illustration is agreed to be imperfect, and each handles that differently. Barnes treats it as simple and blames the expositors: had it been kept in mind that the point is merely that death dissolves the relations which make law binding in life, it would have saved much perplexity and many wild vagaries about men being the wife, the law the former husband and Christ the new one. Such expositions, he says, are enough to make us mourn over the puerile and fanciful interpretations that even wise and good men give to the Bible. Ellicott states the defect precisely instead: the law is represented by the husband, yet the apostle means that the Christian dies to the law and not the law to the Christian, so the proposition must be taken abstractly — relations of this kind are terminated by death, not necessarily the death of one party more than the other. Calvin makes the mismatch deliberate: the apostle might have completed the comparison by saying the law is dead to us, but rather than offend the Jews by the asperity of that expression he turned aside and said we are dead to the law. Wesley dissolves the difficulty: the law is spoken of by a common figure as a person, to which life and death are ascribed as to a husband, and the apostle speaks indifferently of the law being dead to us or we to it, the sense being the same.

The particulars draw shorter notes. Robertson identifies the word for the married woman as a late compound meaning under a husband, found nowhere else in the New Testament. Theodoret guards the charge of adultery: the law calls her an adulteress not who marries after her husband's death but who joins herself to another while he lives. Clarke turns it to use: the change argues no disloyalty to the Maker, since a believer is as free to receive the gospel as such a woman would be to marry again. Henry sets out what the deliverance covers: we are freed from the power of the law that curses and condemns, the sentence being vacated by the death of Christ, and also from the power of the law which irritates and provokes the sin dwelling in us.
4:
Which law is meant divides them. Calvin says the point is incontestable from what follows: it is the moral law and not the ceremonial, since the apostle quotes a moral commandment in the next verse and says that by it sin slew him, which could not be said of the ceremonial law. Clarke reads it the other way, as a transfer to another constitution in which the literal rites and sacrifices are done away. Theodoret agrees: in the flesh means under the polity of the law, the flesh being the ordinances concerning foods and drinks and leprosy.

Two of them guard the deliverance from being taken too far, and reach the same guard from different sides. Barnes lists what Christians are freed from — the law as a means of justification, as a source of sanctification, and as a bondage — then stops: not from it as a rule of duty. Gill enumerates the same releases, from the ministration by Moses, from the covenant of works, from its curse and from its being an irritant to sin, and adds the identical proviso: but not from obedience to it as it is in the hands of Christ.

The text of verse 6 is disputed, and the two who take it up reach the same reading by different roads. Barnes reports a variation in the manuscripts, some reading as though the law were dead and others as though we were, and notes that the majority favour the latter. Ellicott traces the history of the error instead: the translators followed a reading found in no manuscript at all, which arose from a mistake of two editors in interpreting a patristic comment — the true text running, we were delivered from the law, having died to that wherein we were held. Theodoret, long before either, had noticed the same delicacy and given the reason: the apostle continues in his cautious mode of expression, saying not that the law is made to cease but that we are made to cease from the law.

How the release was effected is answered twice over. Ellicott says that in the act of our baptism, which united us to Christ, we obtained release from our old tyrant the law. Theodoret had said it in the same terms — being subjects of the law we came to baptism, and dying with Christ and with him rising again we were united to our Lawgiver. Ellicott adds that the clause about serving expresses result rather than purpose: release from one master implied engagement to another. Robertson puts it plainly: death to the letter has set us free to new life in Christ.

On the effect of the law while it ruled, Calvin is severest. As long as its literal teaching rules unconnected with the Spirit of Christ, the wantonness of the flesh is not restrained but breaks out and prevails, so that those under it attain nothing but this, that their ears are struck by an external sound without fruit or effect. Hence the zealots of the law act unreasonably in wishing to detain the faithful under its dominion, since bondage to the law produces sin only. Theodoret makes a careful distinction there: the apostle says not that the passions were in the law but by the law, for the law does not itself bring about sin but condemns it, sin using for evil what was good — nor do our members bring about sin, but only by our members has the inclination of the soul to the worse brought its operations into effect. Wesley glosses the working in the members as spreading over the whole man, and the sins by the law as accidentally occasioned by it; Clarke gives the plainest account of the yoke, that it sentenced every transgressor to perdition and provided no pardon even for the penitent and no sanctification for those weary of their inbred corruptions.
7:
Wesley answers here the question the chapter is famous for, and answers it flatly. This is a digression in which the apostle, to show the weakness of the law, changes the person and speaks as of himself about the misery of a man under the law — a thing he often does when assuming another character. The character assumed is that of a man first ignorant of the law, then under it, sincerely but ineffectually striving to serve God; and to have spoken this of himself or of any true believer would have been foreign to the whole scope of the discourse, indeed contrary to it. Calvin resists the autobiographical reading at the same point for a different reason, wondering what came into the minds of interpreters to render the passage in a past tense as though the apostle were speaking of himself, when his purpose was plainly to begin with a general proposition and only then explain it by his own example.

What sin is, in a chapter that keeps making it an agent, divides the two who face it. Barnes de-personifies it: sin here means not a real entity, nothing independent of the mind having a separate existence lodged in the soul, but the corrupt passions and inclinations of the mind itself — as we say that lust burns and ambition rages and envy corrodes, without supposing any of them independent subsistences. Perhaps nowhere, he adds, has the apostle shown more consummate knowledge of the human heart. Clarke goes the opposite way and lets the personification stand: sin is represented as a murderer watching for life, snatching at every means and embracing every opportunity to carry his fell purpose into effect — the miserable sinner has a murderer within him.

The phrase rendered taking occasion is glossed three ways, two of them military. Ellicott says the Greek implies a base of operations, an advanced post occupied as the starting-point for further advances, and holds that sin cannot act on a man without the co-operation of law. Theodoret used the same figure: sin made the law a means for battle and beat down the weaker powers of judgment. Robertson prefers a starting-place from which to rush into acts of sin, excuses for doing what men want to do, illustrating it from his own century: drinking men use the prohibition laws as occasions for violating them. Clarke thinks the pointing wrong, the comma belonging after occasion and not after commandment.

Ellicott also asks whether by the commandment attaches to the taking of occasion or to the working in me, and sees reasons for the second. Gill settles what the commandment is: either the whole moral law, or that particular precept thou shalt not covet, which the Jews say comprehends all. Henry states the objection all this answers: having said so much about the law as a covenant, the apostle might be thought to reflect on it, and so shows its excellency — not as a covenant but as a guide — for laws are as the lawmakers are, and God being holy, just and good, his law must needs be so.

On sin being dead before the law came, the notes converge. Robertson makes it exact — dead means inactive, not non-existent, sin being present in a dormant state. Wesley says the same descriptively, that it was neither so apparent nor so active. Theodoret gives the principle, that where there is no law pointing out what should be done and forbidding what should not, sin has no place, and adds the apologetic motive governing the passage: having said that sins were increased by the law, the apostle sets out its manner in every way he can, lest anyone suppose the law their cause. Calvin reduces it to a sentence: the knowledge of sin without the law is buried.
9:
Who the “I” of these verses is divides the catena three ways, and Gill names and rejects the two he does not hold. It is not Adam, who never lived without law and in whom sin could not be said to revive, never having lived before; nor is it Israel before Sinai, who had circumcision and sacrifices. Theodoret holds precisely the first: Adam had no fear of death until the commandment respecting the trees came, whereupon the devil came to the woman in the serpent, she was overcome by desire, and Adam shared the sentence. Clarke, quoting Whitby, holds the second, that the seed of Abraham was alive before the law was given, not liable to a death not yet threatened. Barnes takes it as autobiography — no doubt the apostle refers to his own past experience — while adding that he speaks there the sentiment of every unconverted man depending on his own righteousness.

What that life was, they agree in describing and differ in naming. Barnes makes it a kind of peace, free from the convictions of conscience. Calvin is harsher: inflated with a conceit as to his own righteousness, the man claimed life while he was yet dead — whence the axiom that the death of sin is the life of man and the life of sin the death of man. Wesley says it in the first person: I had much life, wisdom, virtue, strength, so I thought. Robertson borrows Denney’s lost paradise in the infancy of men and Shedd’s a seeming life. Ellicott presses revived: sin did not come to life but came to life again, lurking in the heart from the first and dormant until the commandment arrives.

On the commandment ordained to life, Barnes argues in steps: the law is good, on a being perfectly holy it would produce life only, but it crosses the inclination of a sinner and so yields woe. Gill narrows the promise: immortal life to Adam and life in Canaan to Israel, but never eternal life, which is the free gift of God. Calvin calls the wound incidental, as an incurable disease is exasperated by a healing remedy — inseparable, so that the law is elsewhere called the ministration of death, yet not hurtful in its own nature. Robertson and Ellicott both stop on I found, a passive: it turned out so for me; Theodoret draws from the same word that the intention of the law and the end brought about by sin were widely different things.

At deceived me Clarke hears Eve, the apostle using the very word the Septuagint gives her at Genesis 3:13; and the verb for slaying, he adds, also means to make wretched, so that the sinner lives a dying life, or a living death. Robertson has sin personified as the tempter and renders the slaying bluntly: killed me off. Barnes generalises instead: all sinners are so deceived, urged on headlong by their passions. Calvin alone shifts the deception from the thing to our knowledge of it: we are led out of the way in the sense that the law makes evident how far we had already departed.

The conclusion is drawn wide. Ellicott says the wherefore looks back not to the verse before it but over the last five; Barnes reads it as the answer to the question of verse 7. Calvin takes the three epithets as a point-by-point antithesis to sin: sin works depraved lusts and the law is holy, sin acts the traitor and the law is plain dealing, sin leads to death and the law to happiness. Theodoret alone splits the terms, taking the law for the Mosaic and the commandment for what was given to Adam, and explains the greater praise given the latter by the greater censure it meets. Robertson closes flatly: the modern revolt against law needs these words.
13:
The verse opens an objection, and the notes differ over whose mouth it is in. Clarke makes it a Jew’s, the apostle disputing with a countryman who asks whether the law can be allowed good and still be called the cause of our death. Gill treats it as an objection started and taken out of the mouth of another person, and holds that it rests on a misreading: the apostle had said he died when the commandment came and found it to be unto death, but never that the law caused his death — at most it was an occasion, and the occasion was not given by the law but taken by sin. Barnes states it as a general question, whether that which tends to life can be made death to a man. Calvin says what had until now remained doubtful, namely how nothing but death could be gained from so singular a gift of God, and answers by a distinction: it is through our wickedness that the law is turned to our destruction, but it is not the cause of death in such a sense that death is to be imputed to it.

Calvin then reaches for the harder parallel, the law called in 2 Corinthians 3 the ministration of death, and argues that the phrase represents not the real character of the law but the false opinion of his opponents. The printed note immediately turns on itself — this can hardly be admitted, the apostle there evidently states a fact, and the fact was that the law proved to be the ministration of death, though it proved so through something other than itself. The second voice is the editor’s rather than Calvin’s, and the catena gives no sign of the change of hand.

On the purpose clause the notes converge and press it hard. Barnes reads it as development rather than manufacture: sin was to show its true nature and be no longer dormant, and no man knows his own heart until the law crosses his path and shows him what he is. Robertson makes it grammatical first — a final clause, sin working death as an incidental result — and then blunt: the sinfulness of sin is revealed in its violations of God’s law, the excesses of sin reveal its real nature, and only then do some people get their eyes opened. He also notes that the English hyperbole is simply the Greek word carried over. Clarke draws the practical consequence, that one design of the law was to exhibit the destructive nature of sin, and that without the law applied to the conscience by the light of the Spirit a man could scarcely see the necessity of the death of Christ.

Ellicott turns the figure round at the end: sin’s dominion here was short-lived and no triumph after all, since the very law it took for its stay turned round upon it and condemned it. Theodoret blames the difficulty of the verse on its extreme brevity and supplies the argument — sin is made apparent as evil by the good thing, and it is made apparent by its working death, for from the fruit I know the tree, and seeing death I hate its parent. He adds two things the others leave out: that nature points out sin but the law has more clearly manifested its excessive turpitude, and that the author of sin is the inclination of our own free will to the worse. Wesley keeps it experimental, with inbred sin driving furiously in spite of the commandment and its guilt thereby greatly aggravated. Gill closes on a maxim, that a law which does not condemn is no law at all.
14:
This verse opens the passage the whole chapter is argued over, and the catena splits down the middle. Barnes says plainly that it describes a man under the gospel and the workings of the apostle’s own mind after his conversion, and gives his reasons in order: it is the obvious sense to plain men without a theory to support; it serves the argument, since to make it pre-conversion would repeat what has already been settled and leave open whether the law can sanctify a believer; and the expressions later in the chapter cannot be said by an impenitent sinner. Clarke takes the other side with heat, holding that the apostle personates a Jew under the law, that by I he cannot mean himself or any Christian, and that the contrary opinion has most pitifully and shamefully lowered the standard of Christianity and disgraced its character — adding the argument that if the words held of a believer they would prove the gospel as insufficient as the law. Calvin takes the passage as an example set before us in a regenerate man, in whom the remnants of the flesh are wholly contrary to the law while the spirit would gladly obey. Theodoret refers it to the man who lived before the coming of grace, beset by his passions and not yet given the spiritual help of the new covenant. Wesley refuses the alternative and makes it a process, the whole course of a man reasoning, groaning, striving and escaping from the legal to the evangelical state.

Henry alone states the deadlock as a deadlock. So far does evil prevail here, in a man sold under sin and not performing what is good, that it seems hard to apply the words to the regenerate, who walk not after the flesh; and so far does good prevail, in hating sin, consenting to the law, delighting in it and serving it with the mind, that it is harder still to apply them to the unregenerate, who are dead in trespasses. He therefore expounds it twice over, first of a convinced but unrenewed soul who knows his Lord’s will and does it not, then of a renewed soul still imperfect.

On spiritual there is no such division. Chrysostom points out that the apostle is still defending the law and does it by praise rather than acquittal, calling it spiritual as a teacher of virtue hostile to vice, which leads off from sin of every kind by frightening, admonishing, chastening and correcting; and if the teacher was so admirable, sin came from the listlessness of the disciples. Gill grounds the word in its origin and its reach: it comes from the Spirit of God, reaches to the spirit of man, requires truth in the inward parts, and cannot be obeyed without the Spirit’s assistance. Robertson gives it in a phrase, spirit-caused and spirit-given. Ellicott declines to argue the point at all, since Christians all know it. Calvin argues against a narrower gloss: the word does not merely mean that the law requires the inward affections of the heart, but stands opposed to carnal, so that as flesh means what is sinful and corrupt, spiritual imports what is holy, just and good, and the discord between the natural man and the law is that of darkness and light.

The last phrase draws the sharpest images. Robertson makes it a completed transaction, sin having closed the mortgage and now owning its slave. Ellicott says the sensual part of a man is as much a slave as if he had been sold in the auction mart. Wesley makes the point of the metaphor total enslavement, slaves bought with money being absolutely at their master’s disposal. Theodoret reads it against the prophet’s reproach that for your iniquities have you sold yourselves, and so makes the seller the man himself, who delivered himself up to sin.
15:
Ellicott observes that three different words for doing are used in the passage and that the distinction is hard to carry into English: the one here and at verse 17 is the strongest, a deliberate action thoroughly carried out, while the other two differ as do and practise, single acts against habitual ones. Clarke says the same of the first, a work the agent continues at until it is finished, the word used of working out one’s own salvation.

The clause rendered I allow not is read three ways. Barnes keeps the English, since the Greek is I know not and knowing is sometimes used for approving. Ellicott takes it flatly: I act blindly, without conscious direction of the will, the higher part of me kept down by the lower. Robertson makes it perception rather than volition, a failure to recognise the thing in its true nature. Theodoret supplies the psychology: the man overcome by pleasure, or intoxicated by anger, has no clear perception of sin, and comes to knowledge of the evil only after the passion subsides. Gill narrows what is being confessed — not a notorious crime nor a sinful course of life, but internal lusts and the workings of corruption in the heart.

The old question returns here sharper. Robertson thinks sold under sin turns the scale for the period before conversion, and takes over Denney’s formula that this is the unregenerate man’s experience, surviving at least in memory into regenerate days and read with regenerate eyes. Clarke asks who could assert without blaspheming that this is said of a man in whom the Spirit dwells. Calvin holds the contrary: the case is now that of a man already regenerated, and the apostle presently denies being wholly possessed by sin, which no unrenewed man could say. The editorial matter printed with Calvin adds a catalogue of the rival schemes — a man in a law state, a Jew living between Abraham and Sinai, a fiction representing the law’s effects on Jews and proselytes.

On the consent of verse 16 the notes agree and one refines. Barnes turns it into a test: the struggle itself shows the evil is not loved and the law that condemns it is, and nothing is a more decisive evidence of piety than a long and painful struggle against evil desire. Ellicott says the desire is itself a witness to the excellence of the law. Theodoret says the very hatred of sin was received from the law, so that he bears the law testimony. Wesley notes that the single word good here carries all three of the earlier epithets. Calvin refuses to let the consent be confused with the pagan’s, who sees the better and approves it while following the worse: those subscribe under constraint, their will wholly alienated, whereas the godly man consents with the real and most cheerful desire of his heart. Cyril warns against a perverse use of the words altogether, since the soul came into the world sinless and we now sin of our own free will.

Verse 17 divides on how far the disowning goes. Ellicott finds a real dualism in the soul and refuses to be identified with the lower self. Robertson agrees but will not let it become an alibi, quoting Denney again, that to be saved from sin a man must at once own it and disown it. Calvin says the same negatively: this is not the plea of a man excusing himself, as triflers do who think casting blame on the flesh covers their wickedness. Clarke describes the tenant as a principle stronger than reason, acting in the soul as a tyrant, for which the law has condemnation but no cure; Barnes has sin lodging as in its home, not yet dislodged.
18:
Everything here turns on the qualifying clause. Barnes seizes on it as decisive for the larger question: the careful in my flesh implies something else in the man that was acceptable to God but did not belong to him by nature. Calvin builds the same distinction into a doctrine of the believer, who is divided into two parts, the relics of the flesh and grace; the confession arraigns him as wholly depraved and the modification is added lest the grace that dwelt in him, though no part of his flesh, be slighted. Wesley contradicts this in a line: the flesh here signifies the whole man as he is by nature. Robertson splits the difference, calling the phrase not absolutely good and no complete view even of the unregenerate, the wishing being the better self and the doing the lower. Barnes meanwhile finds in no good thing the strongest possible statement of total depravity and turns it into a rule of self-examination, since what was true of the apostle is true of everyone.

Clarke uses the verse to mount the chapter’s most vehement dissent, and it is aimed at the reading the others take for granted. Some faculties suffered less in the Fall than others, he says, their concurrence being necessary to salvation, and even the most unconcerned about spiritual things have understanding, judgment, reason and will — whence scoffers at revelation have become eminent mathematicians, astronomers and chemists. At the next verse he presses it home: the will is not opposed to good, being found almost uniformly on God’s side while the whole sensual system is against him; it is not the will that leads men astray but the corrupt passions that oppress it; and this almost only friend to God in the human soul has been slandered as God’s worst enemy by men who had this very chapter before their eyes.

Theodoret traces the impotence to the dominion of the passions, introduced by the mortality of the body and strengthened by the indolence of the mind, so that the willingness came from the law while the power is wanting for lack of further help. Henry turns it into a mark rather than a problem: the purer the heart, the quicker its feeling of the sin remaining in it, and the desires to obey increase as a man grows in grace — which he sets against those who make themselves easy about the inward motions of the flesh and, warned by conscience, go on with forethought in the road to perdition.

Verse 19 the notes mostly acknowledge as repetition. Barnes explains it as intensity of interest, the subject placed in every variety of aspect even at the hazard of repeating. Gill states the substance in a sentence, that the man had a will to good but no power of his own to perform. Calvin draws a harder consequence: since the whole course of the godly life is being delineated and not some particular faults, their best works are always stained with blots of sin, so that no reward can be hoped for unless God pardons them; and had the integrity of our nature remained, the law would never have brought death, restoring health being the work of the heavenly Physician.

At the disowning of verse 20 Gill guards against the obvious abuse, saying the inference is drawn not to excuse the man from blame but to trace his sins to their fountain in the corruption of his nature. Robertson guards it the same way, that the true self no longer does the thing and yet responsibility and guilt remain because the struggle goes on. Clarke, describing two principles perpetually contending for mastery, recalls that this self-contradiction led ancient philosophers to suppose a man has two souls, and tells Xenophon’s story of Araspes, who confessed to Cyrus that one soul could not pant after vice and virtue at once.
21:
The word law in verse 21 is the hardest in the chapter, and Ellicott sets out the choice: most take it as rule or habitually repeated fact, the objection being that this gives the word a sense it bears nowhere else in the apostle; the alternative assumes a broken construction, the sentence begun as though it would say the Mosaic law is found unable to help and finished in another form. Clarke takes the first, glossing it as any strong or confirmed habit under whose influence a man generally acts. Barnes takes it the same way while keeping the notion of binding and controlling, though what binds here is not imposed by a superior. Wesley compresses it to an inward constraining power flowing from the dictate of corrupt nature. Calvin instead counts four laws — the law of God, alone properly so called; the law of the mind, the readiness of the faithful mind to obey it; the law of unrighteousness, the dominion iniquity exercises, so named as even a tyrant’s enactments are called laws; and the law of the members, the lust that keeps concord with iniquity. Gill hears the rabbinic evil imagination behind it, whose first name among the seven, he says, is evil. Theodoret solves it by repunctuating, putting a full stop after the wish to do right.

At the delight of verse 22 the chapter’s long dispute reaches its sharpest point. Barnes rests his case on the verb, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means to rejoice with, denoting not assent of the understanding but sensible pleasure of the heart — and never yet did an impenitent sinner find pleasure in contemplating the spiritual law of God. Gill argues the same negatively: the unregenerate dislike the law’s commands and cannot delight in what threatens and curses them, and the moralist or Pharisee obeys externally from fear and for the applause of men. Clarke denies both. Every Jew who receives the Old Testament must acknowledge the excellence of its maxims, though without grace he can never act by them; and to say that the inward man means the regenerate part of the soul is supportable by no argument, the phrase being common in the Greek moralists for the rational part of a man, and paralleled among the Jews, who make the Spirit the inward man whose garment is the body. Ellicott places the inward man midway between the law of the mind and the spirit, and Theodoret makes it simply the mind. Wesley adds only that the day of liberty draws near. Calvin sees in the division the source of the contest between spirit and flesh that Augustine called the Christian struggle.

Verse 23 is read by nearly everyone as a siege. Clarke draws it out furthest: a city besieged and at last taken by storm, the assailant laying continual siege, harassing, battering and storming the spirit, and the inhabitants carried away captive. Robertson supplies the philology, a rare verb for campaigning against and a vivid one for enslavement, calls the picture tragic, and notes that Plato, Ovid, Seneca and Epictetus describe the same dual struggle. Barnes completes the figure from the law of war, since a captive taken was at the disposal of his victor. Theodoret puts the blame on the soul’s own sluggishness, she having cast off her freedom and allowed herself to be subjected, while still hating the servitude she obeys. Cyril takes the verse somewhere else entirely, using it to argue the Incarnation: the devil had used the flesh as an instrument against us, and by the very same weapons the victory was won back. Henry defends the passage against its readers, since it does not represent the apostle as one who walked after the flesh, and no man who has never been engaged in this conflict can rightly judge of it.
24:
The cry is read as a cry, and the notes chiefly ask what is being cried out of. Robertson borrows a phrase for the whole, a heart-rending cry from the depths of despair, adding that anyone who thinks the estimate exaggerated should recall the writer calling himself chief of sinners, since he dealt too honestly with himself for complacency to live long in him. Clarke supplies the image that has stuck to the verse: the wounded captive is not merely surrounded by the slaughtered but chained to a dead body, in allusion to the tyrant who bound corpse to living man, hand to hand and face to face, till the putrid mass killed him — and he quotes Virgil on Mezentius at length. Gill fences the misery about: not as the man is considered in Christ, where he is secure; not as to his inward man, renewed day by day; not as to his future state, of which he had no doubt; nor chiefly on account of persecution, which he took pleasure in; but on account of the continual combat and the mass of corruption he carried about.

What the body of this death is divides them slightly. Ellicott makes the body itself the cause of sin and therefore of death, so that the cry asks release from a whole mortal nature in which appetite, sin and death are mingled, and holds that a triple resurrection, ethical and spiritual and physical, is needed to complete it. Theodoret keeps the same sense but narrows it: it is called a body of death as being born subject to death, the soul being immortal. Wesley makes it this mass of sin, cleaving as close to the man as his body to his soul. Barnes traces the effects rather than the referent: the conflict produces distress and humility, and the mind so overwhelmed sighs for relief — asking whether the law can aid, or man, or any native strength of conscience or reason, and finding all tried in vain. Calvin insists the question is not asked in doubt, as unbelievers ask who do not know there is one deliverer, but is the voice of one panting and almost fainting because help does not come at once; and both he and Wesley note that the verb implies force. Wesley adds the observation the others leave unsaid, that the deliverance is not wrought yet.

At the thanksgiving three of them stop on a variant. Clarke reports that several manuscripts, the Vulgate and some fathers read the grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ for I thank God, which turns the two verses into a question and its answer, and he prints them so. Gill gives the same variant and expounds it as the answer to the earlier appeal, that the grace of God shall deliver me. Calvin weighs the copies and comes down for the received text as the safest course where the context gives no strong reason otherwise.

The close is drawn differently by each. Barnes takes it as the point the whole argument tended to: what conscience and law and unaided strength could not do the gospel has done, and the superiority of the gospel is triumphantly established. Robertson marks the structural division, the obligation to be sanctified proved earlier and its possibility the business of what follows. Ellicott judges the deliverance to be sanctification rather than justification, a freeing from the impulses of sense. Theodoret puts the two ages together: Christ ended death and promised a life apart from labour and warfare, the full enjoyment to come, while the grace of the Spirit is given now as a Helper by which the passions may be triumphed over. Wesley keeps his reading to the end: the I is the person being personated until the deliverance is wrought, and the man, utterly weary of his bondage, stands upon the brink of liberty.
